## The Genomics Data Explosion {.smaller}

[Why we visualize]{.eyebrow}

### Scale of the problem

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}

- <span style="color: #807b6d;">**1 to 2 exabytes** of data produced on YouTube per year</span>

- <span style="color: #208462; font-weight: 700;">220 million genomes</span> sequenced <span style="color: #208462; font-weight: 700;">per year</span>

- Equivalent to <span style="color: #807b6d; font-weight: 700;">40 exabytes</span> per year

- That's more than <span style="color: #208462; font-weight: 700;">20 times</span> more than YouTube produces

::: fragment
For years we struggled to collect biological data, but now our biggest bottleneck is [analyzing and interpreting it]{.alt}

## Why Python for Genomics Visualization? {.smaller .scrollable}

[The Python viz stack]{.eyebrow}

### One language, full pipeline

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Python's strengths in bioinformatics:**

::: fragment
**Ecosystem breadth**

- One language for the full pipeline: parsing → analysis → visualization
- Direct integration with `scikit-learn`, `scanpy`, `biopython`
- Reproducible notebooks with Jupyter / Quarto
:::

::: fragment
**Interactivity out of the box**

- Plotly, Bokeh, Panel for web-ready figures
- DashBio for genomics-specific widgets
:::

::: fragment
**Publication quality**

- Matplotlib + Seaborn: journal-grade static figures
- Fine-grained control over every visual element
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: fragment
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# The whole pipeline in one language
import pandas as pd            # data wrangling
import numpy as np             # numerics
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # static plots
import seaborn as sns          # statistical plots
import plotly.express as px    # interactive plots

# Genomics-specific
import scanpy as sc            # single-cell
from Bio import SeqIO          # sequence parsing
import pyCirclize              # circos plots
import toytree                 # phylogenetics
```
:::

<!-- slide 7 -->
## From ggplot2 to Python — The Mental Map {.smaller .scrollable}

[From ggplot2 to Python]{.eyebrow}

### Same grammar, different syntax

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**ggplot2 (R)**
Built on the Grammar of Graphics — the same ideas power Python's ecosystem.

| ggplot2 | Python equivalent |
|---------|------------------|
| `aes(color=group)` | color kwarg / palette dict |
| `geom_point()` | `ax.scatter()` |
| `geom_line()` | `ax.plot()` |
| `facet_wrap(~group)` | `fig, axes = plt.subplots()` |
| `theme()` | `rcParams` + `ax.set_*()` |
| `scale_color_manual()` | custom `palette` dict |
| `labs()` | `ax.set_title/xlabel/ylabel()` |
| `ggsave()` | `fig.savefig(..., dpi=300)` |

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: fragment
**The key shift in mindset:**

- ggplot2 maps data aesthetics **declaratively** — you describe *what* to show
- matplotlib/seaborn are **imperative** — you describe *how* to draw it
- seaborn bridges the gap with a high-level API closer to ggplot2
- For exploratory work → seaborn; for full control → matplotlib
:::

::: fragment
> Every ggplot2 figure you've made has a matplotlib equivalent.
> The grammar is the same — only the syntax changes.
:::
:::
::::::

<!-- slide 8 -->
## ggplot2 vs Python — Side by Side {.smaller .scrollable}

[From ggplot2 to Python]{.eyebrow}

### A volcano plot in both languages

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
**R / ggplot2**
```r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(df, aes(x = log2FC,
               y = -log10(pvalue),
               color = regulation)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    up   = "#C23B22",
    down = "#2B6CB0",
    ns   = "#888888"
  )) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05),
             linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1),
             linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "VOLCANO PLOT",
       x = "log₂ Fold Change",
       y = "−log₁₀(p-value)") +
  theme_minimal()
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: fragment
**Python / matplotlib + seaborn**
```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

pal = {"up": "#C23B22",
       "down": "#2B6CB0",
       "ns": "#888888"}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))

for reg, grp in df.groupby("regulation"):
    ax.scatter(grp.log2FC, grp.neg_log10_p,
               c=pal[reg], alpha=0.6,
               s=15, label=reg)

ax.axhline(-np.log10(0.05), ls="--",
           color="#CCCCCC", lw=1)
ax.axvline(-1, ls="--", color="#CCCCCC", lw=1)
ax.axvline( 1, ls="--", color="#CCCCCC", lw=1)

ax.set_title("VOLCANO PLOT", fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xlabel("log₂ Fold Change")
ax.set_ylabel("−log₁₀(p-value)")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
```
:::
:::
